title: Pentagon Rewrites Counter-Drone Playbook After Replicating Ukraine-Style Attack in Florida
excerpt: A mock assault at Eglin Air Force Base exposed gaps in U.S. defenses and prompted $600 million in rapid procurement, as the military races to absorb battlefield lessons from Ukraine.
body:
• A U.S. Special Forces unit replicated a Ukrainian "spiderweb" drone attack at Eglin Air Force Base, revealing critical gaps in American counter-drone defenses.
  • The Pentagon has committed over $600 million to rapid counter-drone procurement and is requesting $75 billion for drone technology in the 2027 budget.
  • The U.S. Army is now training with drone-deployed smoke screens to shield advancing armored columns, directly borrowing from Ukrainian battlefield tactics.
  • A new U.S.-Ukraine drone cooperation agreement will allow the Pentagon to evaluate combat-proven Ukrainian drone platforms.

The Florida Exercise That Changed Everything

In a September exercise dubbed Operation Clear Horizon at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida, members of the 10th Special Forces Group launched a drone assault that mirrored the "spiderweb" attack Ukraine had recently staged against Russia. Their targets: counter-drone troops from across the U.S. military, trained for a week on technology the Pentagon has spent billions developing.

https://x.com/Drone_Wars_/status/2087459423660728693

The results were sobering.

"What I would tell you is that it helped us develop our priorities."

— Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, Joint Interagency Task Force 401

The special operators flew drones resistant to jamming, equipped with directional antennas and frequency-hopping connections. They used fiber-optic-controlled drones and, in a first for the U.S. military, piloted drones over the cellular LTE network from Colorado to strike targets in Florida. The exercise covered the full drone spectrum, from small Group 1 systems to larger Group 3 platforms.

From Exercise to Overhaul

The drill exposed a fundamental problem: U.S. drone defenders had no unified system to combine data from far-flung radars, sensors, and counter-drone systems. Within months, the Pentagon developed a single drone-tracking software solution and interface that works across all service branches and partner agencies.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=qEwDezmAaZ8

Between September and December, 67 separate counter-drone tests were conducted across the Defense Department, but their data was siloed. The task force has since created mechanisms for informed, cross-program comparisons.

Ross's team traveled to Ukraine six weeks before his April briefing, observing how Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Force defends Kyiv nightly and studying forward-line tactics. That intelligence now feeds directly into U.S. procurement decisions.

Borrowing Ukraine's Battlefield Innovations

The influence extends beyond counter-drone strategy. During the Spartan Focus 2026 exercises at Fort Stewart, Georgia, the U.S. Army deployed heavy eight-rotor drones fitted with compact smoke-generation modules to shield advancing M2A4 Bradley columns. The concept — drones flying ahead of armored formations to lay smoke over exposed terrain — was adapted directly from Ukrainian combat operations.

At Fort Bragg, soldiers from the Army Marksmanship Unit, 1st Special Forces Command, and the 82nd Airborne Division conducted live anti-drone training using standardized Army weaponry, focusing on engaging both surveillance and weaponized drones with cost-effective, legacy systems rather than million-dollar missiles.

The Scale of Investment

The Pentagon's response has been massive. Over $600 million has been committed to rapid counter-drone technology integration in the past six weeks alone. The 2027 budget proposal requests $75 billion for new drone technology — a sum larger than the annual GDP of some countries and the current budget of the U.S. Marine Corps.

A new U.S.-Ukraine drone cooperation agreement, signed in July, formalizes what had been ad hoc collaboration. Under the framework, the U.S. military can request specific Ukrainian drone platforms — including interceptor drones, electronic warfare systems, and maritime attack drones — for testing and assessment.

"This is a giant leap forward for American defense. I've been saying for five years that the US needs to make a cultural change to learn from Ukraine. This is the first step."

— Dan Rice, President, American University Kyiv

Why Drones Are Not the New IEDs

Ross has pushed back against comparisons between today's drone threat and the IEDs of Iraq and Afghanistan. Unlike roadside bombs, drones benefit from a massive commercial ecosystem that continuously accelerates their evolution.

"For IEDs, you had no commercial application for that technology. With unmanned systems, and specifically with autonomy, there's so many commercial applications that we're going to see this accelerated development," Ross said. "That's going to cause us concerns, from a security perspective."

Offensive and defensive drone operations are "inextricably linked," he added, signaling that the traditional separation between long-range fires teams and missile-defense units must end.
